title: Power outage: first steps
def: When the power goes out, safety comes first: use flashlights, keep fridge and freezer doors shut, unplug electronics, and never run fuel-burning devices indoors.
look: the neighborhood is dark too, or only your home
outside temperature and how long it may last
people who rely on powered medical devices
use: Check on household members, report the outage to the utility, switch off major appliances, and keep phones charged from a power bank or a car run outdoors.
not: Do not use candles where a flashlight will do, or run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors.
steps: Check on neighbors who may need help.

title: Generator safety
def: A portable generator makes deadly carbon monoxide, so it must run only outdoors, at least 20 feet from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from the house.
look: the generator outside, far from openings
a working CO alarm inside
heavy-duty outdoor extension cords
use: Run it outdoors and dry, plug appliances in with outdoor-rated cords, let it cool before refueling, and keep CO alarms working inside.
not: Never run a generator in a home, garage, basement, or shed, even with doors open, and never plug it into a wall outlet to backfeed the house without a transfer switch.
call: Get to fresh air and call 911 if anyone has headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion.

title: Carbon monoxide: alarms, symptoms, and indoor fuel
def: Carbon monoxide is an invisible, odorless gas from burning fuel; it causes headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion, and can kill people as they sleep.
look: several people or pets sick at once
symptoms that improve outside
a fuel-burning device running indoors
use: Put CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas, test them monthly, and get everyone outside at once if an alarm sounds.
not: Never heat or cook indoors with a charcoal grill, camp stove, or generator, and never warm up a car in a closed garage.
call: Get to fresh air and call 911 if anyone has symptoms or the alarm sounds.

title: Drinking water when the well pump or city water is down
def: When the pump or city supply fails, use stored water first, then water from the hot water heater or ice, and treat any other water before drinking.
look: stored water, at least a gallon per person per day
the water heater tank as a reserve
a boil-water notice from the utility
use: Boil water for one minute (three above 6,500 feet), or disinfect clear water with unscented household bleach as the EPA directs, and follow utility notices.
not: Do not drink floodwater or water from a flooded well until it is tested, and do not use bleach with added scents or cleaners.

title: Staying warm without power, and space-heater risk
also: how to stay warm without electricity
def: To stay warm without power, gather in one small room, layer clothing and blankets, and use only heaters rated for indoor use, kept away from anything that burns.
look: one room with doors closed and windows covered
hats, layers, and sleeping bags
space heaters three feet from bedding and curtains
use: Close off unused rooms, eat and drink warm fluids, and if the house gets dangerously cold, go to a warming center or a friend's home.
not: Do not use an oven, grill, camp stove, or generator for heat indoors, and do not leave a space heater running unattended or on an extension cord.

title: Keeping pipes from freezing
def: Pipes freeze where cold air reaches them, such as outside walls, crawl spaces, and garages; a frozen pipe can burst when it thaws.
look: little or no water from a tap in very cold weather
frost on exposed pipes
pipes along outside walls
use: Let faucets drip, open cabinet doors under sinks, and warm a frozen pipe gently with a hair dryer or warm towels, starting at the tap end.
not: Do not thaw pipes with an open flame or torch.
call: If a pipe bursts, shut off the main water valve and call a plumber.

title: Downed power lines
def: Treat every downed line as live and deadly; electricity can travel through wet ground and water around it.
look: a sagging or fallen wire
sparking or buzzing
a line touching a car, fence, or puddle
use: Stay at least 35 feet away and call 911 and the utility. If a line is on your car, stay inside and wait for help unless the car is on fire.
not: Do not touch a person or object in contact with a line, drive over a downed line, or walk through water near one.

title: Flashlights versus candles
def: Battery flashlights and lanterns are far safer than candles during an outage; candles start many home fires.
look: fresh batteries and spare flashlights
candles near curtains, bedding, or children
lights left burning at night
use: Use flashlights or battery lanterns, keep spare batteries, and if you must use a candle, keep it in a sturdy holder, away from anything that burns, and never leave it alone.
not: Do not use candles while sleeping or near children and pets.

title: Home fire escape plan
def: A home fire escape plan gives every room two ways out and an outside meeting spot; in a fire you may have only a couple of minutes to escape.
look: working smoke alarms on every level and in sleeping areas
two exits from each room
a meeting place outside
use: Practice the plan twice a year, get out fast and stay out, crawl low under smoke, and call 911 from outside.
not: Do not go back inside for anything, and do not open a hot door.
steps: Feel doors; use another way if hot.

title: If you smell gas
def: A rotten-egg smell can mean a natural gas or propane leak, which can explode from a single spark.
look: a rotten-egg or sulfur smell
hissing near a gas line or appliance
dead plants over a buried line
use: Leave right away, leaving doors open behind you, then call the gas utility or 911 from a safe distance outside.
not: Do not flip light switches, use phones, start cars, or light anything inside or near the leak.
call: Call the gas utility or 911 from outside.

title: Medicines and medical devices during an outage
def: People who rely on powered medical devices or refrigerated medicines need a plan for outages: backup power, a cooler, and a place to go.
look: oxygen, CPAP, dialysis, or other powered equipment
insulin or other medicines that need cold
battery runtime for each device
use: Register with your utility as a medical priority if offered, keep backup batteries charged, and plan where to go if power will be out long.
not: Do not use medicines that look changed after heat or freezing without asking a pharmacist.
call: Call 911 if a person dependent on a device is in danger.

title: When to stay home and when to leave
def: Stay home when it is safe, warm or cool enough, and supplied; leave when officials order an evacuation or when your home is no longer safe.
look: an evacuation order from local officials
no heat in freezing weather or no cooling in extreme heat
rising water, fire, or a gas leak
use: Follow local officials, leave early if you need extra time, and take your kit, medicines, documents, and pets.
not: Do not wait to see if it gets worse when told to evacuate, and do not drive through floodwater.
